method: Full independent reread of all25 current frozen items and prior findings, including clinical text, every option/rationale, key, takeaway and revised metadata. Statuses manually reasoned; exact snapshot hashes preserve the reviewed inputs. No clinical-text carry-forward was inferred from metadata-only claims.
limitations: Independent AI editorial/clinical-reasoning screen; not external clinician validation or psychometric validation.
Pass applies only to the recorded content hash. New or changed content requires further review.
No comparison against proprietary examination items; originality judged from author provenance and item content.
Cross-bank learning-objective overlap remains provisional until all batches are available.
Source checks below support only the explicitly associated claims; other category references are general reading unless specifically verified.

items.assessment: Changed strength makes barcode alert investigation meaningful; current order/product comparison resolves the discrepancy before dosing. Old dose, unrelated barcode and postadministration repair do not.
Prompt accountable disposal and replacement addresses severe pain without false administration records or unattended controlled-drug storage.
Stable client with a reported undocumented dose needs administration-history verification. A blank record or stable pressure cannot exclude duplicate exposure.
A1.8mL dose cannot be accurately measured in5mL cup graduations; the fine calibrated oral syringe addresses a concrete device mismatch.
Timing alone does not determine retained absorption after emesis; drug-specific guidance is safer than a full/half replacement or independent interval change.
Assessing nausea and agreeing acceptable treatment respects refusal and addresses current tolerability. Isolated nausea does not establish immune allergy or justify permanent class avoidance.
Single-dose designation remains relevant for same-client future doses; routine storage or bedside pre-drawing is not an authorized sterile preparation process. Foundation label is honest.
Organizer placement and an old list do not establish product identity/current authorization. Verified identification and intent avoid both duplication and prolonged unexplained omission.
Old-patch removal plus time/site recording directly address duplicate exposure; same-site reuse, applying before checking and reconstructed memory records fail the stated problem.

Hand support corrects observed tip contact without promoting corneal placement or imprecise delivery. Foundation label fits; contaminated-product disposition would additionally follow product/local instructions.
Separate original calculations followed by comparison preserve independence; hearing the first result biases the check. Both selected actions fit a policy explicitly requiring this check.
Individual tube suitability no longer implies mixing compatibility. Separate medicines and prescribed flushing accommodate both dose delivery and fluid restrictions.
The key is sound, but “only possible explanation” makes the dosing-error alternative trivially dismissible. A concrete possible duplication is a better competing hypothesis.
issues: The key is sound, but “only possible explanation” makes the dosing-error alternative trivially dismissible. A concrete possible duplication is a better competing hypothesis.

options: A duplicate administration during the medication round
Accumulation despite an unchanged prescribed dose
Reduced absorption caused by the creatinine rise
Tolerance requiring a higher dose
why: A duplicate dose remains a possible cause to investigate, but the stated renal decline specifically supports reduced clearance even with correct administration.
Reduced clearance can increase exposure even when administration has not changed.
The main stated change affects elimination rather than proving poor absorption.
New drowsiness during renal decline suggests increased effect, not reduced response.

items.assessment: Option0 advertises its omission (“only…without reviewing”), making the safe assessment key easier to guess. Use a plausible incomplete monitoring focus.
issues: Option0 advertises its omission (“only…without reviewing”), making the safe assessment key easier to guess. Use a plausible incomplete monitoring focus.

options: Check blood pressure and review whether orthostatic dizziness is present
Reassess after the client has completed a full sleep cycle
Assess sedation and breathing before further sedating doses
Give the next sedative because respirations exceed 12/min
why: Blood pressure and postural symptoms may be relevant, but they do not assess progressive sedation and ventilation after adding another central depressant.
Waiting may miss progressive sedation and ventilatory impairment.
Combined effects can progress, so current safety and the regimen need review.
A single respiratory rate does not establish safety with increasing sedation.

items.assessment: A postinfusion sample cannot be interpreted as the ordered trough. Reporting exact times allows appropriate repeat sampling and dosing review rather than unplanned withholding or reduction.
The safety context is now adequate, but the respiratory-rate alternative announces itself with “only evidence”. Keep the safety measurement without spelling out its insufficiency.
issues: The safety context is now adequate, but the respiratory-rate alternative announces itself with “only evidence”. Keep the safety measurement without spelling out its insufficiency.

options: Ask about nausea and assess tolerance of a small permitted intake
Record sleep as proof that nausea resolved
Measure respiratory rate and compare it with the predose value
Wait for a full meal before reassessing
why: This measures the target symptom and its functional effect.
Sedation can occur without relief of nausea.
Respiratory monitoring evaluates medication safety; it does not directly establish nausea relief or tolerance of permitted intake.
A smaller permitted intake can evaluate response sooner and more tolerably.

items.assessment: Unknown compatibility is correctly resolved before co-infusion. Option0 signals deliberate nonassessment, rather than a realistic administration alternative.
issues: Unknown compatibility is correctly resolved before co-infusion. Option0 signals deliberate nonassessment, rather than a realistic administration alternative.

options: Pause the maintenance fluid and give the medicine through the same tubing
Verify compatibility and an appropriate administration method
Run the medicine slowly through the Y-site
Look for cloudiness after starting the medicine
why: A pause does not establish compatibility with residual solution or an appropriate flushing/interruption plan; the infusion purpose and administration method still need verification.
The nurse needs a safe plan before the solutions contact each other.
A slower rate cannot establish chemical compatibility.
Some incompatibilities are not visible, and exposure has already occurred.

items.assessment: Physical bag-to-client tracing resolves detached labelling among similar infusions; pump location, remaining volume and an old diagram are meaningful but unreliable proxies.
New painful resistance correctly triggers stopping use and assessment. Remove the explicit “without reassessment” giveaway from the repositioning distractor.
issues: New painful resistance correctly triggers stopping use and assessment. Remove the explicit “without reassessment” giveaway from the repositioning distractor.

options: Use a smaller syringe to generate more pressure
Reposition the arm and begin the medicine at a slower rate
Flush until blood return appears
Stop using the catheter and assess the site and patency
why: Higher pressure can damage the catheter or surrounding tissue.
Changing position or rate does not establish patency or resolve the cause of new pain and flushing resistance.
Continuing against resistance can worsen a catheter complication.
New pain and resistance suggest a complication requiring assessment.

items.assessment: Vein-tracking warmth/redness/tenderness favour phlebitis over cool localized infiltration or an adhesive pattern. Foundation difficulty appropriately describes this recognition question.
The named sublingual formulation depends on the prescribed mucosal route; swallowing, chewing or mixing into a drink does not reproduce it. Foundation label is appropriate.
The spacer key addresses observed coordination failure, but two distractors explicitly announce missing assessment. Replace those omission cues with plausible incomplete interventions.
issues: The spacer key addresses observed coordination failure, but two distractors explicitly announce missing assessment. Replace those omission cues with plausible incomplete interventions.

options: Rehearse the written press-and-breathe sequence before the next dose
Arrange a dry-powder inhaler to remove the press-and-breathe step
Trial a compatible spacer with return demonstration
Add extra puffs to compensate for estimated loss
why: The client has already had repeated coaching; repeating the sequence does not directly address the demonstrated timing barrier.
A dry-powder device may be suitable for some clients, but inspiratory ability and device suitability must be assessed; a compatible spacer directly addresses this demonstrated barrier.
A spacer reduces the timing coordination required for delivery.
The delivered amount remains uncertain and the prescription is altered.

items.assessment: Two alternatives are wrong merely because they say unlabelled or unidentified. Use plausible but incomplete equipment/identification safeguards so the key requires selecting the route-specific combination.
issues: Two alternatives are wrong merely because they say unlabelled or unidentified. Use plausible but incomplete equipment/identification safeguards so the key requires selecting the route-specific combination.

options: Label a Luer syringe for oral use and place it by the feeding pump
Use a labelled enteral syringe and select the line nearest the feeding pump
Use a labelled Luer syringe and have a second nurse confirm the drug
Use a labelled enteral syringe and trace the tube
why: Labelling and location cannot prevent a vascular connection when equipment is compatible with IV access.
Dedicated equipment and a label help, but equipment position does not verify which tube reaches the intended enteral route.
A drug check does not remove the vascular connection risk of using IV-compatible equipment for an enteral dose.
Dedicated equipment and tracing reduce wrong-route connection risk.

items.assessment: Prompt pharmacy contact and escalation protects time-critical continuity. Independent timing or drug substitution and passive restocking delay do not resolve the current supply risk.

The ordered elbow treatment does not authorize use on new facial redness. Review protects against wrong diagnosis/site; a thinner or previously prescribed weaker steroid does not resolve authorization.
